theme: I delight to do your will, obedience better than sacrifice
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 40:1-10. Yesterday’s psalm said that God wants thanksgiving more than sacrifices. Today’s goes further, with a line that the New Testament applies to Christ. Read verses 6 to 8 slowly.
settingTheScene: Psalm 40 is a psalm of David. The first ten verses are a song of thanksgiving for being rescued, and the rest of the psalm is a prayer for help. In the first part, David describes how God brought him out of a pit and put a new song in his mouth. Then, in the middle of the thanksgiving, he says something that seems surprising in a week spent reading about sacrifices: God has not desired sacrifice and offering.
observation: “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry” (v. 1).
“He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure” (v. 2).
“He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD” (v. 3).
“Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust” (v. 4).
“Sacrifice and offering you have not desired, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required” (v. 6).
“Then I said, Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me” (v. 7).
“I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (v. 8).
“I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, O LORD” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a rescue story. David was in a pit, a bog, and he could not get out. He waited, and God lifted him up and put him on solid ground. The result is a new song. A person who has been rescued cannot help singing. And the song is for others, too: “Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD.”

In verses 6 to 8, David reflects on what God wants in return. His answer echoes Psalm 50, Psalm 51, and the prophets. It is not mainly sacrifice. What God wants is an open ear and a willing heart. “You have given me an open ear.” The Hebrew phrase is literally “ears you have dug for me,” the picture of a God who opens the ears of his servant so he can hear and obey. “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.” It sounds like the promise of the new covenant in Jeremiah 31:33, where the law is written on the heart.

David does not say that the sacrifices are worthless. He says that they are not what God ultimately desires. The sacrifices were always meant to be accompanied by obedience, and obedience is what they were pointing to. “In the scroll of the book it is written of me” may mean that David sees his own kingship described in the law (Deuteronomy 17:18-20). But the language is larger than David could fill. He is a king who delights in God’s will, but not perfectly. His words reach beyond him to the perfect obedient servant.

The psalm ends the section with public witness. David does not keep his rescue to himself. He tells the “glad news” in the great congregation. A rescued person speaks. He declares God’s faithfulness and steadfast love, and does not hide it.
connection: Hebrews 10:5-10 quotes Psalm 40:6-8 and puts the words on the lips of Christ as he comes into the world: “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me.” Jesus is the one who fully delights to do God’s will. He says, “I have come to do your will, O God.” And by that will, “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” The sacrifices were always pointing to someone who would offer himself with a willing heart.
application:
Think back to a time when God lifted you out of a pit. Tell someone the story this week.

Ask the Lord for an open ear and a heart that delights in his will, not just one that obeys.

Read Hebrews 10:5-10 and thank Jesus for coming to do the Father’s will on your behalf.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for drawing you out of the pit and setting your feet on a rock.
Ask him for an open ear and a heart that delights in his will.
Thank Jesus for coming to do the Father’s will for you.
